# The Argument

A chart is a claim about how the world is organised. The scatter that became
the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram claims that a star's brightness and colour are
not independent; the map Snow drew of Broad Street claims that cholera deaths
have a centre; Anscombe's four little panels claim that a summary statistic is
not a substitute for looking. The history of scientific visualisation is not a
history of decoration — it is a history of structural claims that happened to
be made with ink.

The claims succeed or fail through the eye. Human vision resolves a small set
of channels before attention gets involved — position, length, size, colour,
orientation, motion — and resolves them with sharply different precision;
position on a common scale is read almost losslessly, area and colour
saturation are read with systematic bias [@cleveland1984graphical]. Bertin
catalogued these channels as a grammar of marks [@bertin1967semiologie], and
the catalogue explains why the same data can be legible in one encoding and
mute in another. The first part of the Atlas walks through the channels one at
a time, each illustrated not by a toy but by the canonical figure that made
the channel famous.

Perception does more than measure single marks — it groups them. Marks that
connect read as one structure; marks that flow read as a path; marks that sit
close, or look alike, read as a cluster; a boundary read as enclosure turns
space itself into an encoding. These Gestalt principles are the load-bearing
walls of the network diagram, the Sankey, the heatmap, and the map, and they
organise the second part. The third part leaves the static frame: systems that
move, figures that animate, and the honest depiction of what is not known —
uncertainty drawn rather than suppressed.

Provenance is treated as data. *First* and *canonical* are distinct facts: the
treemap is introduced at a 1991 conference but cited from a 1992 journal
article, and conflating the two is the most common error in visual-history
writing. Each Atlas entry therefore declares its provenance class — a named
first, a canonical reference, a shared genre idiom with no single inventor, or
an attribution that remains contested — and backs the claim with a citation
that must resolve for the entry to exist. Some famous forms are excluded on
principle: the supply–demand cross and the political compass are conceptual
diagrams, not depictions of measured data, and this book catalogues only forms
that show the world rather than a theory of it.

What the catalogue adds up to is the book's argument: the sciences do not
share a subject matter, but they share a visual language, and that language is
small. A few perceptual channels, a few grouping principles, a few honest ways
to draw a distribution or a flow or a doubt — the whole of organised knowledge
is drawn with them.
